title: British Airways Probes Food Poisoning After All Three Pilots Fall Ill on Hyderabad Flight
excerpt: One first officer was incapacitated at 30,000 feet and put on oxygen during the 10-hour flight to Heathrow. The airline is now reviewing crew accommodation in Hyderabad after its pilots' union flagged dozens of prior hygiene complaints.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • All three pilots on a British Airways flight from Hyderabad fell ill with suspected food poisoning.
  • An urgent investigation is underway after prior hygiene complaints about the hotel were reported.
  • One pilot required oxygen at 30,000 feet; symptoms worsened after landing in London.
  • British Airways operates 63 weekly flights from five Indian cities to Heathrow, including Hyderabad.
Pilot Health Crisis Mid-Flight
›All three pilots fell ill during a 10.5-hour flight.
›One first officer incapacitated at 30,000 feet.
›Symptoms worsened after landing in London.
›All pilots filed Air Safety Reports.

British Airways has launched an urgent investigation after all three pilots on a Boeing 777 flying from Hyderabad to London Heathrow fell ill with suspected food poisoning mid-flight, according to The Sun and The Economic Times.

One first officer was "incapacitated" at 30,000 feet during the 10½-hour flight and had to be placed on oxygen, the reports said. The remaining two pilots managed to continue flying the aircraft, but their symptoms worsened after landing in Britain.

"An urgent investigation has been launched as this must not happen again."

— Source close to British Airways, via The Sun

Hotel Hygiene Under Scrutiny

The three pilots had shared breakfast and drinks in the lounge of their £130-a-night layover hotel in Hyderabad before the flight, according to The Sun. All three drank bottled water provided by an external company. The food consumed at the hotel is now the primary focus of the investigation.

Insiders at the British Airline Pilots' Association (Balpa) told The Sun that officials are "furious" because there had been "dozens" of previous complaints about hygiene standards at the Hyderabad hotel used by BA crews. All three pilots have filed Air Safety Reports and were asked to provide medical samples so doctors could pinpoint the contamination source.

A British Airways spokesperson confirmed the review in a statement: "The welfare of our colleagues is a top priority and we are reviewing crew accommodation in this location following some isolated reports of sickness."

Crew Moved to New Accommodation

Balpa confirmed that the airline has already relocated pilots to alternative lodging in Hyderabad. "Balpa reps work extensively to ensure that hotels for staff are of a high standard and that the accommodation, location and amenities meet the needs of pilots," a union spokesperson said. "We have worked extremely closely with British Airways in recent years to ensure hotels meet the needs of flight crews and we will continue to do so. This includes moving pilots to alternative accommodation in Hyderabad within the past days."

The Economic Times reported that a pilot became unwell during a Hyderabad-to-London Heathrow flight "earlier this week," and that the aircraft continued safely to its destination, landing normally. BA said flight safety was not compromised at any point.

What It Means for Travellers on the India-UK Route

Hygiene Complaints Under Review
›Dozens of prior hygiene complaints reported by pilots' union.
›Pilots shared breakfast and drinks at a £130-a-night hotel.
›Investigation focuses on food consumed at the hotel.
›Crew relocated to alternative accommodation in Hyderabad.

British Airways operates 63 weekly flights to London Heathrow from five Indian cities — Delhi, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Hyderabad, and Chennai — with daily services from Hyderabad and Chennai. The Hyderabad-London route uses Boeing 777 wide-body aircraft for the long-haul service.

While the airline stressed that flight safety was not compromised, the incident raises questions about crew welfare protocols on India routes and the oversight of ground-level logistics such as hotel and catering arrangements for foreign airline crews operating in Indian cities.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those on the heavily used Hyderabad-London corridor, the episode is a reminder that operational safety extends well beyond the aircraft itself. Hyderabad's Rajiv Gandhi International Airport is a major hub connecting southern India's technology workforce with the UK.

BA's investigation will seek to identify the exact source of contamination — whether from food, water, or the hotel environment. The medical samples provided by the pilots are being analysed. The airline is also expected to review its crew accommodation standards across all Indian stations.

Aviation regulators have not publicly commented on the incident, but the filing of Air Safety Reports means the data will be available to both the UK Civil Aviation Authority and India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation for review.
